# Slow sand filtration and chlorination of town water (`water_filtration_chlorination`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/medicine.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Medicine & hygiene (`medicine`)
- Deps: helped by chlorine_bleach, cholera_waterborne, contagion_theory
- Core idea: A town can treat its water centrally. Let the water stand in a settling basin, then run it slowly downwards (10–30 cm of water depth per hour) through a bed of fine sand about a metre deep resting on gravel and drain pipes. After one to three weeks a slimy living layer grows on the sand surface and removes almost all germs; the bed must stay wet and running, and is cleaned by scraping off the top centimetre. Chlorine demand varies. For clear water below pH 8, check that at least 0.5 mg/L of free chlorine remains after at least 30 minutes of contact. Some parasites resist ordinary chlorination, so filtration still matters. Hamburg, which drank unfiltered Elbe water, lost about 8,600 people to cholera in 1892; Altona next door, with sand filters, was nearly spared.
- Pitfalls:
  - Filtering fast through coarse sand or cloth, which clears the water but leaves the germs
  - Letting the filter run dry or scraping away the whole living layer and using the water at once
  - Thinking charcoal makes water safe; it removes taste and smell, not disease
  - Dosing chlorine by guess: too little does nothing, far too much is undrinkable; muddy water uses the chlorine up
  - Placing the intake downstream of the town's own sewers
- History: india: early centuries AD – the Sushruta Samhita describes clarifying turbid water with materials including cloth and kataka seeds (dating disputed); europe: 1804 – Gibb's sand filter, Paisley; 1829 Simpson's slow sand filters, Chelsea Waterworks, London; 1852 filtration required for London's river water; 1892 Hamburg and Altona; 1897 emergency chlorination at Maidstone; 1902 continuous chlorination at Middelkerke, Belgium; americas: 1908 – Jersey City (Leal and Fuller) chlorinates a whole city supply; typhoid in American cities collapses within a decade
- Read:
  - M. N. Baker, The Quest for Pure Water (1948)
  - L. Huisman and W. E. Wood, Slow Sand Filtration (World Health Organization, 1974)
  - Michael J. McGuire, The Chlorine Revolution (2013)
